questions.question: Which of the following crops is commonly grown in dry, arid areas and requires minimal water?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Bajra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Bajra**, also known as **pearl millet**, is a widely cultivated grain in India, especially in **dry and arid regions**.
 
• It is a **drought-resistant crop** that requires minimal water for cultivation, making it ideal for **semi-arid and arid climates**.
 
• Bajra is primarily grown in states like **Rajasthan, Gujarat, Haryana, and Maharashtra**.
 
• It is a hardy crop with the ability to grow in **poor-quality soils** and under extreme temperatures.
 
• Bajra is a rich source of **essential nutrients** such as iron, magnesium, and protein and is often used as a staple food in regions with limited water availability.
 
• It has a short growth cycle and can be harvested in **2-3 months**, making it a reliable crop for farmers in water-scarce regions.
 
• In addition to human consumption, Bajra is also used as **fodder** for livestock, contributing to the agricultural economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Rice**__

 __
 
• Rice is a **water-intensive crop** that requires a significant amount of water for cultivation.
 
• It is primarily grown in regions with **high rainfall** or where irrigation systems are well-developed.
 
• Major rice-growing states in India include **West Bengal, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, and Andhra Pradesh**.
 
 
 
• **Jute**__
 __
 
• Jute is a **fiber crop** that thrives in warm and humid climates with plenty of water.
 
• It is mainly grown in the **Ganges delta** regions of **West Bengal, Assam, and Bihar**.
 
• Jute is used to make products like **gunny bags, ropes, and mats**.
 
 
 
• **Wheat**__
 
 
• Wheat is a major **rabi crop** grown in cooler climates, typically during the winter season.
 
• It requires moderate water and is cultivated in states like **Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh**.
 
• Wheat is a staple food crop and is used to produce **flour, bread, and other food products**.

questions.question: What role does infrastructure play in agricultural development?

options.text: Ensures better irrigation, storage and transportation facilities

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ensures better irrigation, storage and transportation facilities**__.

__
 
• **Infrastructure in agriculture** enhances productivity by providing **adequate irrigation facilities**, ensuring consistent water supply for crops.
 
• Efficient **storage facilities** prevent post-harvest losses, safeguarding farmers’ produce and improving their incomes.
 
• Improved **transportation systems** enable timely movement of agricultural products to markets, fostering better price realization for farmers.
 
• Infrastructure development promotes **access to modern technology**, mechanization, and inputs, leading to sustainable agricultural practices.
 
• It facilitates **export opportunities** by ensuring quality preservation and compliance with global standards, boosting the agricultural economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Irrigation Infrastructure:** Involves canals, dams, tube wells, and drip irrigation systems to ensure optimal water usage and increase crop yield.
 
• **Storage Facilities:** Includes warehouses, cold storage units, and silos to reduce spoilage and maintain the quality of produce post-harvest.
 
• **Transportation Networks:** Roads, railways, and ports play a vital role in connecting rural farms to urban markets, reducing time and costs.
 
• **Mechanization:** Access to tractors, harvesters, and other machinery improves efficiency and reduces labor dependency in agriculture.
 
• **Supply Chain Management:** Effective supply chain systems ensure seamless integration from production to consumption, benefiting both farmers and consumers.

questions.question: What is the local name used for the primitive form of cultivation (slash and burn agriculture) in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Podu**__.

__
 
• **Podu** is a traditional form of **shifting cultivation** practiced by tribal communities in the Indian state of **Andhra Pradesh**.
 
• This method involves **clearing a patch of forest** through slash-and-burn techniques, cultivating the land for a few years, and then allowing it to regenerate.
 
• The term **Podu** is derived from the local dialects and is common among tribes like the **Koya**, **Chenchu**, and other indigenous groups.
 
• This practice is particularly followed in the **Eastern Ghats** region of Andhra Pradesh, where the terrain and soil conditions are suitable for such cultivation.
 
• Although traditional, this method has been criticized for its impact on **deforestation, soil erosion, and biodiversity loss**.
 
• Efforts are being made by the government to **promote sustainable agricultural practices** and reduce dependency on shifting cultivation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Dahiya**__

 __
 
• **Dahiya** refers to a form of shifting cultivation practiced in some parts of **Madhya Pradesh** and adjoining states.
 
• This method is similar to Podu but is identified by a different local term in those regions.
 
 
 
• **Bringa**__
 __
 
• Bringa is the local term for shifting cultivation (also known as slash-and-burn agriculture) in the state of Odisha, India. 
 
 
 
• **Valre**__
 
 
• **Valre** is not recognized as a term related to any traditional agricultural practices in India.

questions.question: In India, 'Rabi' crops are sown from:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**October to December**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Rabi crops** are typically sown in India during the **winter season**, starting from **October to December**.
 
• The crops are cultivated in regions with **cooler temperatures**, as these conditions are favorable for their growth.
 
• Examples of Rabi crops include **wheat, barley, mustard, peas, and gram**, which are harvested around March to April.
 
• The irrigation system plays a crucial role in Rabi crop farming, as it primarily depends on **residual moisture** from the monsoon season.
 
• These crops are also referred to as **"winter crops"** because they are sown after the end of the monsoon season.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kharif crops**: These are monsoon crops, sown from **June to July** and harvested around **September to October**. Examples include rice, maize, and cotton.
 
• **Zaid crops**: These are summer crops grown between the Rabi and Kharif seasons, from **March to June**. Examples are watermelon, cucumber, and fodder crops.
 
• The term "Rabi" originates from the Arabic word for **"spring"**, as these crops are harvested in the spring season.
 
• India's diverse agro-climatic zones allow for the cultivation of a wide range of crops, enabling year-round agricultural productivity.
 
• Government initiatives such as the **Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY)** aim to improve irrigation facilities and boost Rabi crop yields.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of Slash and Burn agriculture and its state is correctly matched?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kumari – Assam**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Kumari** is a traditional form of slash-and-burn agriculture practiced in the state of **Assam**.
 
• This agricultural practice involves clearing forested land by cutting and burning vegetation to create fields for cultivation.
 
• It is primarily practiced by tribal communities in the northeastern region of India, including Assam.
 
• In Assam, it is commonly associated with hilly or forested regions where shifting cultivation is feasible.
 
• The crops typically grown using this method include rice, millet, and vegetables suited to the local terrain and climate.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Slash-and-Burn Agriculture Overview**

 
 
• A traditional farming technique where forests are cleared by cutting down and burning trees and vegetation.
 
• It is also referred to as shifting cultivation, as farmers move to a new plot once soil fertility declines.
 
 
 
• **Regional Names in India**
 
 
• **Kumari** – Assam
 
• **Jhum** – Northeastern states like Nagaland, Meghalaya, and Mizoram
 
• **Penda** – Madhya Pradesh and Andhra Pradesh
 
• **Podu** – Odisha and Andhra Pradesh
 
• **Bringa** – Odisha
 
 
 
• **Environmental Impacts**
 
 
• Leads to deforestation and biodiversity loss in the area where it is practiced.
 
• Soil fertility depletes over time, making the land less productive after repeated cycles.
 
• Contributes to carbon emissions due to vegetation burning.
 
 
 
• **Government Initiatives**
 
 
• The government has introduced programs to encourage sustainable farming practices and reduce dependence on slash-and-burn methods.
 
• Efforts like agroforestry and integrated watershed management aim to balance ecological sustainability with agricultural productivity.

questions.question: Identify the group of crops which is grown in Kharif Season in India?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Urad and Cotton**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kharif crops** are typically sown at the onset of the **monsoon season** in India, which begins in June, and harvested in the months of September and October.
 
• **Urad (black gram)** and **Cotton** are important crops grown during the Kharif season due to their suitability for the climatic conditions associated with monsoons.
 
• **Cotton** thrives in regions with high temperatures and moderate rainfall, which are typical during the Kharif season.
 
• **Urad** is a leguminous crop that grows well in the warm and humid conditions during Kharif, particularly in states like **Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Rajasthan.**
 
• Kharif crops require abundant water and are often dependent on **rain-fed agriculture** in India.
 
• Other major crops grown in the Kharif season include **rice, maize, jowar, bajra, tur (arhar), moong, soybeans, and groundnut.**
 
• The sowing of Kharif crops aligns with the arrival of the **Southwest Monsoon**, ensuring adequate water supply for their growth.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Groundnut and Barley**__

 __
 
• **Groundnut** is grown during both Kharif and Rabi seasons, but it is predominantly a Kharif crop due to its dependence on monsoon rainfall.
 
• **Barley**, on the other hand, is a Rabi crop and is sown in winter (October-November) and harvested in summer (March-April).
 
 
 
• **Gram and Mustard**__
 __
 
• **Gram (Chickpea)** and **Mustard** are both Rabi crops, which are grown in the winter season and harvested before summer.
 
• These crops require cool weather and relatively less water compared to Kharif crops.
 
 
 
• **Jute and Wheat**__
 
 
• **Jute** is a major Kharif crop grown in regions like West Bengal, Bihar, and Assam due to high rainfall and warm climatic conditions.
 
• **Wheat**, however, is a Rabi crop and is cultivated during the winter season.

questions.question: The fertile alluvial soils of the Great Indian Plains are mostly suited for the cultivation of:
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**rice and wheat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Great Indian Plains** are known for their **alluvial soils**, which are formed by the deposition of silt brought by rivers such as the Ganga, Yamuna, and their tributaries.
 
• **Alluvial soil** is highly fertile and rich in nutrients such as **potash, phosphoric acid, and lime**, making it ideal for **agriculture.**
 
• The region is well-suited for the cultivation of **rice and wheat** due to its favorable **climatic conditions**, such as adequate rainfall and moderate temperatures.
 
• **Rice** is a water-intensive crop and thrives in areas with **high rainfall** and an abundant water supply, which the Great Indian Plains provide.
 
• **Wheat**, on the other hand, is a rabi crop and grows well in the dry and cooler conditions of the winter season, which are also characteristic of this region.
 
• The Great Indian Plains serve as the **granary of India**, contributing significantly to the country’s food security through the production of these staple crops.
 
• States such as **Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, and Bihar** are major producers of rice and wheat, benefiting from the fertile plains.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Coffee and Tea**__

 __
 
• **Coffee and tea** are typically cultivated in regions with **hilly terrain** and a **tropical climate**.
 
• These crops require **well-drained soils** with high organic content, which is not a characteristic of the Great Indian Plains.
 
• Major coffee-producing regions in India include **Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu**, while tea is predominantly grown in **Assam, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, and Kerala.**
 
 
 
• **Pulses and Oilseeds**__
 __
 
• **Pulses** and **oilseeds** are typically grown in regions with **less fertile soils** and in areas that receive **less water**.
 
• The Great Indian Plains are primarily used for high-yield crops like rice and wheat rather than pulses and oilseeds.
 
• Major regions for pulse and oilseed cultivation include **Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Rajasthan.**
 
 
 
• **Cotton and Tobacco**__
 
 
• **Cotton** requires **black soil**, which is commonly found in regions like **Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Madhya Pradesh**, not in the alluvial plains.
 
• **Tobacco** grows well in **light sandy soils** and requires a warm climate, with regions like **Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, and Gujarat** being significant producers.

questions.question: According to the 2011 Census, what was the male literacy rate in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**82.14%**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• According to the **2011 Census of India**, the male literacy rate was recorded at **82.14%.**
 
• The literacy rate measures the percentage of people aged 7 and above who can read and write with understanding in any language.
 
• The overall literacy rate in India in 2011 was **74.04%**, with male literacy being higher than female literacy.
 
• The female literacy rate in 2011 stood at **65.46%**, highlighting a gender gap in education.
 
• Kerala recorded the highest male literacy rate at **96.11%**, while Bihar had the lowest at **71.20%**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Definition of Literacy:**

 
 
• As per the Census of India, a person aged 7 years and above who can read and write in any language with understanding is considered literate.
 
• This definition does not take into account formal schooling or educational qualifications.
 
 
 
• **Gender Gap in Literacy:**
 
 
• The gender gap in literacy rates in India is a key challenge, with male literacy consistently higher than female literacy.
 
• In 2011, the gender gap in literacy was approximately **16.68%**.
 
 
 
• **Efforts to Improve Literacy:**
 
 
• Government initiatives like **Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan** aim to enhance access to quality education across genders.
 
• Programs such as **Beti Bachao Beti Padhao** focus on reducing the gender disparity in education.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• India's literacy rate has shown consistent improvement over the decades, rising from **18.33%** in 1951 to **74.04%** in 2011.
 
• However, rural-urban disparities in literacy persist, with urban areas exhibiting higher literacy rates.

• The population density of India has shown a steady increase in every census due to factors like **population growth** and **urbanization.**
 
• India is one of the most densely populated countries in the world, with states like **Bihar** (1102 persons per km²) and **West Bengal** (1028 persons per km²) having the highest population densities in 2011.

• The increasing population density has significant implications for resources, infrastructure, and governance in India.
 
• The **2011 Census** data also highlighted the rapid growth of urban areas, contributing to higher population density in metropolitan cities like **Delhi** (11,297 persons per km²).
 
• The **National Population Policy** aims to address concerns related to high population density by promoting family planning and enhancing resource management.

• **Population density** is a crucial metric for policy-making as it impacts resource allocation, infrastructure planning, and environmental sustainability.
 
• Higher density areas often require more investment in **transportation, housing, and public services** to cater to the needs of the population.
 
• Low-density areas may face challenges in **economic development** due to limited workforce and infrastructure.
 
 
 
• **Population Growth Challenges**__
 
 
• India's growing population density has increased pressure on **natural resources** such as land, water, and forests.
 
• Overcrowding in urban areas leads to issues like **traffic congestion, pollution, and inadequate housing.**
 
• Efforts to manage population growth include awareness campaigns and policies promoting **education, health care, and family planning.**

questions.question:
Which of the following are the categories to measure the level of Human Development of the countries?

1. Very High

2. Medium

3. Low

4. Below Average
questions.solution:

__
 
• The **Human Development Index (HDI)** is a composite index developed by the **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)** to measure and rank countries based on their level of human development.
 
• HDI categorizes countries into **four broad levels of human development**, namely:
 
 
• **Very High Human Development** – Countries with a high HDI value (close to 1.0).
 
• **High Human Development** – Countries that are progressing but not at the highest level.
 
• **Medium Human Development** – Countries with moderate progress in human development.
 
• **Low Human Development** – Countries that lag in key indicators of human development.
 
 
 
• In the given question, the categories "**Very High**", "**Medium**", and "**Low**" are accurate classifications used in the HDI framework.
 
• The option "**Below Average**" is not a recognized category in the HDI framework, making it incorrect.
 
• The correct answer includes only the valid HDI categories: **Very High, Medium, and Low.**

 __

• Examples include **Norway, Switzerland, and Ireland**, which often rank at the top of the HDI.
 
 
 
• **Medium Human Development**__
 __

• Examples include countries like **India, Ghana, and Vietnam.**
 
 
 
• **Low Human Development**__

questions.question: A settlement with fewer than 5,000 people is classified as _____.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**a village**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A settlement with fewer than 5,000 people is typically classified as a **village** in many countries, including India.
 
• Villages are generally rural areas with low population density and limited infrastructure compared to towns and cities.
 
• In India, a village is administered by a local self-governing body known as the **Gram Panchayat**.
 
• Villages are often characterized by traditional lifestyles, agriculture-based economies, and close-knit communities.
 
• The classification of settlements (village, town, city) varies by country and is determined by population thresholds and administrative policies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gram Panchayat:**

 
 
• The local governing body at the village level in India, established under the Panchayati Raj system.
 
• It is responsible for managing local issues such as water supply, sanitation, and rural development.
 
 
 
• **Town Classification:**
 
 
• A settlement with a population greater than 5,000 but typically less than 100,000 is categorized as a town in India.
 
• Towns often have better infrastructure and services compared to villages.
 
 
 
• **City Classification:**
 
 
• A city is a large and densely populated urban settlement with advanced infrastructure and administrative importance.
 
• In India, cities are often classified based on population (e.g., Tier 1, Tier 2 cities).
 
 
 
• **Administrative Divisions in India:**
 
 
• India is divided into states, districts, and further into smaller administrative units like talukas, towns, and villages.
 
• Districts are larger administrative units that may encompass multiple towns and villages.

questions.question: Which of the following is mainly labour-intensive farming and utilises high doses of biochemical inputs and irrigation to obtain higher production?

__
 
• Intensive subsistence farming is characterized by a high input of labor to maximize the yield from small land holdings.
 
• This type of farming employs high doses of biochemical inputs such as fertilizers and pesticides to enhance productivity.
 
• Irrigation is extensively used in intensive subsistence farming to ensure water availability for crops throughout the year.
 
• The primary aim of intensive subsistence farming is to achieve maximum crop output to support the farmer's family and generate surplus for market sale.
 
• Crops commonly grown in this farming system include rice, wheat, and other grains essential for food security in densely populated regions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dryland Farming**

 
 
• Dryland farming is practiced in arid regions where irrigation is not typically used, relying primarily on rainfall.
 
• Crops grown include millet, sorghum, and pulses which are drought-resistant.
 
• The focus is on conserving soil moisture and managing natural resources efficiently.
 
 
 
• **Commercial Plantation**
 
 
• Commercial plantation farming involves growing crops like tea, coffee, rubber, and sugarcane on large estates.
 
• It is capital-intensive and focuses on export-oriented products.
 
• This system uses modern agricultural practices, including mechanization and advanced irrigation techniques.
 
 
 
• **Primitive Subsistence Farming**
 
 
• Primitive subsistence farming is practiced on small patches of land using primitive tools like hoes and digging sticks.
 
• It relies on natural rainfall and does not use modern inputs like fertilizers or pesticides.
 
• Crops include tubers, grains, and vegetables mainly for the farmer's family consumption.

questions.question: In which of the following months are Rabi crops mostly harvested in the northern part of India?

• Rabi crops require a cool climate for growth and depend on irrigation rather than monsoon rainfall.
 
• The harvest season of Rabi crops is crucial to India's agricultural calendar, especially in the northern region.

• These crops require less water and thrive in cool and dry weather conditions.
 
 
 
• **Difference Between Rabi and Kharif Crops:**
 
 
• **Rabi crops:** Sown in winter (October–December) and harvested in summer (April–June).
 
• **Kharif crops:** Sown in the rainy season (June–July) and harvested in autumn (September–October).

• The **geographical spread** of rural areas often makes it challenging to develop infrastructure effectively.
 
• The majority of rural settlements depend on **primary economic activities**, such as agriculture, livestock rearing, and fishing, which do not always demand extensive infrastructure.
 
• Government initiatives like **Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY)** have been launched to improve rural connectivity and infrastructure.
 
• Despite efforts, a significant gap remains in **infrastructure development** between urban and rural areas, leading to issues like migration to cities in search of better opportunities.
 
• Limited access to infrastructure also results in **poor living standards** and slower economic development in rural regions compared to urban areas.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Economic activities are mainly based on the tertiary sector**__

 __
 
• This is incorrect because in rural settlements, the economy is predominantly based on **primary sector activities** like agriculture, animal husbandry, and forestry, rather than tertiary sector activities such as services and trade.
 
• The **tertiary sector** is more prominent in urban areas where there is a higher demand for services like education, healthcare, and retail.
 
 
 
• **High population density**__
 __
 
• Rural settlements typically have a **low population density** compared to urban areas, as they are spread over vast areas with fewer people per unit of land.
 
• Urban areas, on the other hand, exhibit **high population density** due to limited space and high demand for resources and housing.
 
 
 
• **High-rise buildings**__
 
 
• High-rise buildings are a characteristic feature of **urban areas** where land is scarce and vertical development is necessary to accommodate a growing population.
 
• Rural settlements, by contrast, are known for their **horizontal spread** with single-story or low-rise structures, often made from locally available materials.

questions.question: According to the Census 2011, which of the following union territories of India has the least population density?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Andaman and Nicobar islands**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Andaman and Nicobar Islands is a union territory of India located in the Bay of Bengal.
 
• According to the Census 2011, it has the lowest population density among all the union territories of India.
 
• The population density of Andaman and Nicobar Islands is 46 persons per square kilometer.
 
• This low population density is primarily due to the geographical spread of the islands and the limited land available for settlement.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Population Density**

 
 
• Population density refers to the number of people living per unit area of land, usually expressed as persons per square kilometer.
 
• It is an important demographic measure that helps in understanding the distribution of population across different regions.
 
 
 
• **Census 2011**
 
 
• The Census of India 2011 was the 15th National Census since 1871.
 
• It provides comprehensive data on various parameters including population density, literacy rate, sex ratio, and more.
 
• The data is collected and analyzed by the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India, under the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India.
 
 
 
• **Union Territories**
 
 
• Union territories are regions that are governed directly by the Central Government of India.
 
• They have a different administrative structure compared to states and are administered by a Lieutenant Governor or an Administrator appointed by the President of India.
 
• As of now, India has 8 union territories.
 
 
 
• **Geographical Spread**
 
 
• The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are a group of islands at the southeastern edge of the Bay of Bengal.
 
• They are known for their diverse ecosystem, including tropical rainforests, mangroves, and coral reefs.
 
• The islands are spread over an area of approximately 8,249 square kilometers, contributing to their low population density.

questions.question: According to the Census of India 2011, which of the following groups of states recorded a population of more than 30 crore?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• According to the Census of India 2011, Uttar Pradesh recorded a population of approximately 200 million people.
 
• Maharashtra, as per the same census, had a population of around 112 million.
 
• The combined population of Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra exceeds 30 crore (300 million).
 
• These two states are the most populous in India, with Uttar Pradesh being the most populous state followed by Maharashtra.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Census of India**

 
 
• The Census of India is a decennial event conducted by the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
 
• The primary objective of the census is to collect data on the population, which is used for various planning and policy decisions by the government.
 
• The first census in India was conducted in 1872, and since then, it has been carried out every ten years.
 
• The data collected includes demographic details such as age, sex, literacy, occupation, and housing conditions, among others.
 
 
 
• **Population Statistics**
 
 
• Population statistics are vital for understanding the distribution and composition of people in different regions, which helps in resource allocation and development planning.
 
• High population density in states like Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra indicates higher demand for infrastructure, healthcare, education, and other services.
 
• Population data also helps in identifying trends and predicting future growth, which is crucial for sustainable development.
 
• Accurate population statistics are essential for electoral processes, as they determine the representation of different regions in the legislative bodies.
 
 
 
• **Demographic Transition**
 
 
• Demographic transition refers to the transition from high birth and death rates to lower birth and death rates as a country develops from a pre-industrial to an industrialized economic system.
 
• This transition typically occurs in four stages: pre-transition, transition, post-transition, and modern stability.
 
• India is currently in the third stage of demographic transition, characterized by declining birth rates and a steady decline in death rates.
 
• This stage results in a population explosion, as seen in states like Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra, which necessitates effective population control measures and planning.

questions.question: Which of the following years is called the great divide year because of the all time low population of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1921**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The year 1921 is considered the "Great Demographic Divide" in India because it marked a turning point in the country’s population growth.
 
• Before 1921, India’s population growth was slow, with high mortality rates keeping the population in check. Post-1921, the country entered a phase of consistent population growth due to declining mortality rates and better health services.
 
• Great Demographic Divide (1921):
 
 
• The Census of 1921 recorded a slight decline in India’s population, but post-1921, the country’s population grew at an unprecedented rate.
 
• Improvements in medical facilities, sanitation, and public health programs were some of the key factors behind the decline in mortality rates after 1921.
 
 
 
• Pre-1921 Era:
 
 
• Before 1921, population growth was stagnant or slow due to high mortality rates caused by famines, diseases, and lack of medical facilities.
 
 
 
• Post-1921 Growth:
 
 
• From 1921 onward, the population saw consistent growth, leading to a demographic transition that continues today, with India's population surpassing 1 billion by the turn of the 21st century.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Mortality Decline:

 
 
• The rapid population growth post-1921 was mainly due to a decrease in mortality rates, which outpaced the decline in birth rates.
 
 
 
• Population Policies:
 
 
• India introduced family planning initiatives in later decades to manage this population growth, with mixed results in different regions of the country.
